newsitem.title: USA: Klein would examine future phone mergers.
newsitem.headline: Klein would examine future phone mergers.

text.p: Joel Klein told the Senate Judiciary Committee Tuesday he would closely examine any proposed future telephone mergers if he wins confirmation to head the Justice Department's antitrust division.

During the confirmation hearing senators from both parties offered effusive praise of Klein's qualifications. But Klein also was asked to comment on telephone mergers in light of his unconditional approval of the $20 billion Bell Atlantic Corp.-Nynex Corp. merger last week.

Sen. Patrick Leahy called Klein's decision to approve the merger disappointing. In a written statement given to reporters, the Vermont Democrat said Klein's decision shook his confidence in "rigorous oversight and enforcement."
But Leahy was far gentler when he questioned Klein, asking why the Justice Department had approved the merger.
Klein replied, "Bell Atlantic and Nynex were not competing with each other at the time of the merger, they were restricted by law to separate territories."

Klein, who has been the acting head of the antitrust division, said the Justice Department spent a year looking at more than 1 million documents and interviewing numerous witnesses to consider possible antitrust violations. One key consideration was whether the two companies might compete in the future if they remained separate.
"It was my conclusion that this merger would not have an anti-competitive effect," he said.
Earlier Klein was asked in writing whether he met with with Vance Opperman, a Democratic fundraiser who headed the West publishing company before it merged with Thompson Corp. of Canada.
In his written answer to Sen. Charles Grassley, an Iowa Republican, Klein said he had never met with Opperman but that an investigation of West was continuing.
But for the most part Klein had an opportunity to listen to praise.

Chairman Orrin Hatch, a Utah Republican, said Klein was "as fine a lawyer as any nominee who has come before this committee." Sen. Edward Kennedy, a Massachusetts Democrat, said in a written statement that Klein was "well qualified."

And Hatch solicited the advice of Klein on what approach he should take to removing the antitrust exemption from the baseball industry. Klein said he would review a bill that Hatch and others introduced earlier this year and give his opinion to Hatch.
